title: Justice for every life, and a door open to forgiveness.
subtitle: Ending double standards, honoring mercy
then: Ibn Kathir explains that before Islam a stronger tribe would {trap}value its own people's lives at double{/trap} and take less for the weaker. The verse ordered justice and an end to such twisting. It also opened room for the victim's family to forgive, which Qatadah called {reward}a mercy not given to any nation before.{/reward}
now: Most of us will never stand in a courtroom over a life. But you know the smaller version: the rules that bend for the boss's nephew, the cousin whose wrongs are always excused. {idea}The verse refuses that.{/idea} And when you have been wronged, it holds open a door: {reward}forgiving, then settling things kindly.{/reward}
old: Some people's wrongs matter less because of who they are.
new: Every life weighs the same before Allah, and forgiving is honored as mercy.
try: Notice one place where you excuse someone close to you but not others. Even it out.

title: In justice there is life.
subtitle: Why fairness protects everyone

key.label: What it feels like vs what it does

then: The verse speaks to {idea}people of understanding.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains the sanctity of life is preserved because a would-be killer holds back, knowing justice will reach him. He notes the earlier saying that killing stops killing, and that the Quran put it {reward}far more clearly: in it there is life.{/reward}
now: A class where the teacher lets bullying slide. A workplace where theft is ignored. Everyone feels less safe. {idea}When fairness is sure, people hold back from harm.{/idea} Justice is not the opposite of mercy. It is what keeps others alive and safe.
old: Being strict about justice is just being harsh.
new: Fair consequences protect lives and keep people from harming each other.
try: Be fair today in one small decision, even if it is less comfortable than letting it slide.

title: Think of your family before death comes near.
subtitle: Leaving wealth with fairness and care
then: Ibn Kathir explains this verse came before the detailed verses on inheritance, which later gave each heir a fixed share. He cites Ibn 'Umar: after hearing the Prophet ﷺ speak about having a will ready, {idea}no night passed without his will kept with him.{/idea} And a hadith warns that {trap}an unjust will can spoil a lifetime of good.{/trap}
now: Families split over a house, a bank account, a gold set no one wrote down. Siblings stop speaking at the funeral. {idea}A little honest planning, done in health, is a kindness to the people you love.{/idea} Ask a knowledgeable person how to do it rightly.
old: Thinking about what I leave behind can wait until I am old.
new: Caring for my family includes leaving things fair and clear.
try: Write down one thing your family would need to know if you were gone tomorrow.

title: Changing a dead person's words is on the one who changes.
subtitle: The trust of someone who can no longer speak
then: Ibn Kathir includes {trap}adding, deleting, or hiding{/trap} the bequest. Ibn 'Abbas said {reward}the dead person's reward is preserved by Allah{/reward}, while the sin falls on those who changed it. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing: He knows what was said and what was done with it.
now: Your late father told the family who should get his old car. It would be easy to "forget." The paper is in your drawer. {idea}The dead cannot defend their words. Allah heard them.{/idea}
old: No one will know if I quietly change what they wanted.
new: Allah heard what was entrusted, and He sees what I do with it.
try: Keep one promise you made to someone who has passed away, or to someone not present to check.

title: Making peace to fix an unfair wish is a good deed.
subtitle: When correcting is not betraying
then: Ibn Kathir notes a will can carry errors, sometimes {trap}out of the kindness of the heart without thinking of the consequences{/trap}, sometimes by intention. The verse allows someone to {idea}reconcile the parties and set it right{/idea}, so fairness and the deceased's wishes are both respected. That is why it is set apart from the previous verse.
now: Your aunt's wishes leave one sibling out, and everyone is angry. You could pick a side. Or you could sit them down and help them find something fair together. {idea}Being the peacemaker in a family storm is honored.{/idea}
old: Stepping into a family dispute will only make me a target.
new: Helping people reach fairness and peace is a good deed, not interference.
try: If two relatives are at odds, send each a kind word today without taking sides.

title: Fasting was given so you may become mindful.
subtitle: An old practice with one aim
then: Allah addresses the believers and tells them fasting was {idea}prescribed for those before them too.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says fasting purifies and cleanses the soul from bad behavior, and that it {reward}narrows the paths of Shaytan.{/reward} The goal named in the verse is taqwa.
now: Day three of the fast. You are irritable in traffic, snapping at the kids before iftar. The hunger is real, but the verse is pointing past it. {idea}If the fast leaves you a little more careful with your tongue, it is doing its work.{/idea}
old: Fasting is about getting through the day without food.
new: Fasting is training to be mindful of Allah in everything, not only food.
try: Pick one habit, like a sharp word, and "fast" from it today too.

title: A limited number of days, with room for the weak.
subtitle: Built so the heart does not break
then: Ibn Kathir notes fasting was set for a fixed number of days {idea}so it does not become hard on the hearts{/idea} and weaken their resolve. The verse makes room for the sick and the traveller. Ibn 'Abbas spoke of the elderly who struggle to fast, and Anas in old age {reward}fed thirty poor people.{/reward} The detailed rulings are for scholars to explain.
now: Your grandmother insists on fasting though the doctor worries. Your friend on a night shift feels guilty for struggling. {idea}The verse was shaped with weakness in mind.{/idea} Ask someone knowledgeable about your situation, and do not mistake Allah's room for failure.
old: If I cannot do it the hard way, I am failing.
new: Allah built fasting with care for the weak. His room is part of the gift.
try: Check on one elderly or ill person you know during the next fasting days.

title: Allah wants ease for you, not hardship.
subtitle: The month of the Quran, and the spirit of it
then: Allah honored Ramadan by choosing it to send down the Quran, {idea}a guidance for people.{/idea} Even inside the command to fast, the verse says {reward}Allah intends ease for you.{/reward} Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ: make things easy and do not make them hard; give good news and do not drive people away.
now: Your cousin is new to praying and you correct every small mistake. Your teenager is struggling with the fast and you lecture instead of help. {reward}The verse sets the tone: ease, not hardship.{/reward} {idea}Make the way to Allah lighter for those around you.{/idea}
old: Faith is supposed to feel heavy, so the harder the better.
new: Allah wants ease for me, and I should carry that ease to others.
try: Help someone with their fast or prayer today in an easy, encouraging way.

title: When they ask about Me: I am near.
subtitle: No middleman between you and your dua
then: Placed in the middle of the fasting verses, Allah answers the question Himself: {reward}I am near.{/reward} When the Companions raised their voices in takbir, he ﷺ told them {idea}you are not calling one who is deaf or absent.{/idea} Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith that the fasting person's dua until he breaks his fast is not rejected.
now: You think you need the right words, the right place, a holy person to ask for you. You whisper in the kitchen while the rice cooks. {reward}He is nearer than you think.{/reward} {idea}Do not grow impatient and say "I asked and nothing happened."{/idea}
old: My dua is too small or my words too plain to be heard.
new: Allah is near and answers, in His way and His time.
try: Make one dua today in your own words, right where you are, before you break your fast or sleep.

title: They are a garment for you, and you for them.
subtitle: A relief, and a picture of marriage
then: Al-Bara' reported that Qays bin Sirmah worked his land while fasting, {trap}fell asleep before he could eat{/trap}, and fainted the next day. This verse brought relief, and the Companions {reward}were very delighted.{/reward} In it, Allah calls spouses {idea}a garment for each other{/idea}, which Ar-Rabi' explained as cover.
now: Your spouse knows your worst moods and keeps them private. You warm each other through long nights with a crying baby. {idea}A garment covers, protects, and stays close.{/idea} When you talk about each other to friends, ask if you are covering or exposing.
old: My spouse is just the person I share responsibilities with.
new: We are each other's covering: closeness, comfort, and protection.
try: Cover one of your spouse's faults today instead of mentioning it, or say one kind thing about them to someone.
